claims.text: As-cast HfNbTaTiZr possesses an inherent dislocation network.
Pre-straining followed by controlled annealing can produce HfNbTaTiZr samples with enriched or reduced dislocation densities.
Engineering dislocation-network density alters the high-temperature yield behavior of HfNbTaTiZr.
Engineering dislocation-network density alters the thermoelastic recovery of HfNbTaTiZr.
The dislocation network modifies the activation of dislocation glide during high-temperature loading.
The dislocation network modifies recovery processes during high-temperature loading.
Changes in dislocation glide and recovery govern high-temperature yield stress.
Changes in dislocation glide and recovery govern thermoelastic recovery.
Dislocation mobility increases at service temperatures.
Increased dislocation mobility modifies the elastic response and plasticity of HfNbTaTiZr.
Dislocation-engineered samples are predicted to show a measurable shift in yield stress relative to the as-cast state.
Dislocation-engineered samples are predicted to show a distinct thermoelastic recovery modulus relative to the as-cast state.
A quantitative correlation between TEM-measured dislocation density and mechanical or thermoelastic response would support the proposed mechanism.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply between 800°C and 1100°C under controlled strain rates.
Outside the specified thermal or mechanical regime, other microstructural evolution may dominate the response.
Microstructural factors introduced by the thermo-mechanical treatments may also affect the measured responses.
